stories.body:
Relatives try to piece together information found online and from Nepal as Tibet advocates groups say information is suppressed in China

F an Hong last heard from her husband on the morning of the Nepal-Tibet disaster. More than a week later, the 31-year-old is desperately searching for information about Lin Bo, who was working on a Chinese highway project in Nepal. Struggling to get information from authorities, Fan turned to social media for help.

“My husband works on a project in Nepal, about 5 kilometres from the Gyirong border crossing. I want to know what the situation is, but I haven’t been able to reach him,” the 31-year-old from China’s Sichuan province wrote on Rednote.

Her post has gained more than 18,000 likes and nearly 4,600 comments. She is one of many in China with missing loved ones trying to piece together information they are finding online, as Tibetan advocate groups say information is being suppressed on that side of the border.

Lin began working on repairing the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi Highway – which links Nepal to Tibet, China, through the Gyirong border crossing – in 2024. He had been living on site and working on a 16km stretch of the road.

Fan says that rescue missions into the construction site have stalled. She says relatives of survivors are asking the Chinese authorities for permission to send up their own drones or helicopters to look for the missing.

“I feel more disheartened with each passing day. Feel colder and colder inside,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t even have any tears left.”

It is just over a week since the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages and killing more than 1,200 people. On Wednesday, 4,216 remained missing, according to Nepal officials. Chinese authorities say 541 remain unaccounted for on the Tibetan side, including 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries.

The relatively low official death toll from the Chinese authorities has also raised some concern among Tibetan advocacy groups, given the scale of the destruction seen in video footage. “All we can do is imagine – and that should terrify us,” said Tenzin Choekyi from Tibet Watch. As of Thursday, China had officially reported 21 people killed.

While in China, the official narrative heavily focuses on rescue efforts, online posts across Chinese social media show an emotional outpouring of grief and mourning. On Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, photographs of missing border inspection officers are shared under the hashtag “Salute to heroes guarding the nation’s gateway”.

In China, families with missing loved ones say they are relying on information from Nepal, as well as foreign embassies and social media. Tibetan advocate groups say information on the Tibetan side of the border remains heavily restricted.

On 30 August, Tibetan police reported that 10 people had been punished for spreading what authorities called “false information” about the scale of the disaster online.

“This crackdown is obstructing not just public reporting of the disaster and relief efforts but the basic work of establishing whether communities are alive and receiving the support that they need,” said Tencho Gyatso, president of the US-based Tibetan advocacy group the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT)

“Sources are now afraid to speak to outside groups including ICT. One source told ICT it was “extremely unsafe” to speak. Another asked us not to make further contact given the potential ramifications,” she said.

Fan says she is mainly relying on information from Nepal.

“Everyone seems to have forgotten about the workers on the Syaphrubesi–Rasuwagadhi Highway project … All the news coverage is about the hydropower station [in Nepal].

Families of foreign tourists who went missing in Tibet are also desperately searching for information,

British nationals Sridhar Avvari, 43, his wife, Deepti, 41, and their 14-year-old son Abhinav went missing near the immigration area at Gyirong on 26 August, close to the Nepal-Tibet border. The family lives in India and relatives believe they over on to the Tibetan side.

In a call to the family days earlier, Deepti Avvari told them that there would be no signal but would talk when she returned to an area with network activity. After the flash flood, calls to Deepti’s phone stopped connecting.

“There was no signal, so we can’t talk … After coming down, I will call you again,” Deepti told Priyanka Rapaka, her sister in law.

They are desperately waiting for updates.

“We didn’t get any information from China … We are checking online only who are rescued and … how many are dead,” Rapaka said.

Chinese authorities say they are now able to reach the main disaster zone by road. According to state media they are describing the region as an active search and rescue operation and are searching for hundreds of missing people.

Naresh Goyal is anxiously waiting for news about his sister, Neetu Goyal Tiwari, a 51-year-old missing British national who flew from India to Kathmandu on 14 August to join an Isha Foundation pilgrimage.

“The last message received is that they have reached Gyirong immigration office. “They said they are going to check out.” He says he found his sister’s name on a list of missing people circulating on social media, but said he is unsure where the list originated. Getting information out of the Chinese authorities has been difficult.

“Whenever we ask the China government, they are telling us that they will update us through the embassy of the UK,” he says.

“It is very painful here Now we have spent at least seven days and every minute we are waiting,” Goyal says.

stories.title: Trump White House just tossed a grenade into international space relations
stories.summary: "Let me be clear: America is not only welcome—we want you there."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“Let me be clear: America is not only welcome—we want you there.”

The normally genteel world of international space policy turned ugly this week as several prominent US space companies—including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, K2, and Starcloud—pulled out of a high-profile French space summit organized by the country’s president, Emmanuel Macron.

Politico first reported the diplomatic turmoil, saying that the White House “pressured” US space companies to skip Macron’s space summit in Paris next week. Since then, the companies have largely pulled out of the meeting without commenting publicly, though some US representation remains on the two-day program .

Multiple sources confirmed to Ars that an official with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, or OSTP, led the call with US space companies late last week. The call was convened in response to queries from US industry about the French meeting, which is not part of the traditional circuit of international space conferences.

What is the Space Summit?

Macron announced his plans for the meeting during a June 2025 speech on the importance of space to defense and Europe’s need to remain competitive in the domain. He said France would hold a “Space Summit” at the beginning of 2026 to consolidate French and European strategy in space and “mobilize our public and private partners from around the world.” Later, Macron announced that some of France’s most visible space officials, including astronaut Thomas Pesquet and entrepreneur Hélène Huby, would serve as special envoys.

The meeting subsequently slipped from the spring to the fall, and in the meantime, US companies received invites to attend. As is customary in such situations involving geopolitics, the government relations officials with these companies reached out to the White House OSTP with questions about the nature of the summit.

The White House officials were growing concerned that this was not a normal space industry trade show or conference but would instead include some policy prescriptions around contentious issues such as sharing of spectrum. US officials believed that at the end of the summit, European space officials may move to adopt some policies that were not necessarily beneficial to US companies.

This led to the teleconference with the OSTP and some US space companies late last week, during which the government relations officials were advised that the US firms should not necessarily expect to be treated fairly and might be pressured to endorse policy positions that misrepresent their preferences. The companies were not told they must pull out by the Trump White House but were instead advised that attending might not be in their best interests.

After news broke of this call with US space companies, France’s cabinet-level space minister, Philippe Baptiste, still urged the Americans to attend. “Let me be clear: America is not only welcome—we want you there,” he said on X . “This summit brings all major space powers to the table—science, exploration, security, telecom, SSA, and everything that matters.”

By then it was too late.

So what does all this mean?

For the US space companies, it was a relatively easy choice to pull out. For many of these firms, the US government is one of the most important customers, if not the most important, and it’s bad business to ignore the customer’s wishes. But they also look to Europe as an important source of revenue. As Europe looks to build up its communications and defense capabilities in space, it would be expected to buy a lot of satellite buses, star trackers, and other services from the vibrant US commercial space industry. Now, those cross-Atlantic relationships will become more painful, and Europe will likely incentivize buying anything but US space products.

For the White House, there likely was a dual motivation at work. On one hand, US policy officials recognize that the commercial space industry is a major strength of this nation, running laps around Europe and keeping America ahead of China in space. That is worth protecting. But the White House pressure campaign also serves the aims of President Trump, who has decided that he wants to antagonize traditional US allies and seemingly aid Russian President Vladimir Putin in his efforts to undermine NATO. In some corners of the White House, “Europe” has become a dirty word. So keeping major US players away from Macron’s space meeting was a convenient way to embarrass the French leader.

This all feels very unfortunate and unnecessary. Traditionally, space has been a unifier when it comes to geopolitics, with the International Space Station and its partnership that spans Russia, the United States, and the whole of Europe only being the foremost example.

But as it trods a divisive geopolitical course, the Trump Administration has evidently decided that it’s best to use even this tool as a wedge rather than a bridge.

stories.title: Trump calls for interest rate cut after jobs figures raise hike bets
stories.summary: The president's remarks came as stronger-than-expected jobs figures added to growing expectations that rates could be increased.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 September 2026, 13:54 BST

Donald Trump has called for interest rates to be cut later this month, claiming higher rates put the US at a "very unfair disadvantage".

The president's remarks came as stronger-than-expected jobs figures in the US added to growing expectations that rates could be increased, with inflation still running high and American households feeling the pinch of rising prices.

The number of roles added to the economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast by analysts, driven by a boost in hospitality and education hiring.

Trump said the US should have the "LOWEST RATE of any country in the World".

"The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen!", the president said in a post on social media , external .

Last week, Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US central bank, signalled that rates could be hiked if policymakers were not confident price rises were easing for Americans.

Inflation, which measures price increases over time, remains above the Fed's 2% annual target, with prices up 3.4% in the past 12 months, according to the latest data.

The next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. Rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row, but concerns over inflation remain due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

On Friday, US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on average, compared to $3.71 a year ago.

But despite the cost of living rising, wages also appear to be increasing. In August, average hourly earnings for all employees were $37.75 on average, having increased 3.1%.

"Even the most committed dove would struggle to find anything in the August employment report to justify keeping interest rates unchanged," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

He added that the strength in the jobs market meant that the latest inflation figures released next week would only need to be moderately above the Fed's target to fuel expectations of a September hike.

"A hike in rates just became a bit more likely," said Neil Birrell, chief investment office of investment firm Premier Miton.

Almost 60% of traders were betting on an interest rate hike in September, according to CME Group's "FedWatch" data.

An increase in employment during the final month of the summer in restaurants and bars, as well as in local government education ahead of the new school year, was behind August's labour market rebound.

Weaker job figures released earlier in the summer were revised up by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, revealing a stronger labour market than previously thought. Instead of the economy being deemed to have shed 23,000 jobs in July, some 44,000 were found to have been created in subsequent estimates.

While many more jobs were added, the US unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.1% last month, with seven million out of work. Both measures have changed little over the year.

In response to the stronger jobs figures raising expectations of a interest rate hike, US stock market indexes were trading down on Friday.

Trump called the response "crazy". "We just got GREAT Numbers on Jobs, the Market should go UP, because our Credit and Economy are better but, as always, for the past 25 years, the Stock Market goes DOWN, because we're living under False Reality that if things are good, you've got to "KILL IT" because of a "fear" of Inflation," he said.

stories.title: ‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?
stories.summary: From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences When Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences

W hen Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will.”

Perhaps not surprisingly, his bellicose words did not soothe fractious bond markets, and his resumption of the bombing campaign against Iran only made matters worse.

The past fortnight has seen a wave of instability sweeping through government bond markets in major economies – with knock-on effects for millions of borrowers. The interest rate, or yield, on 10-year US government borrowing hit 4.8% on Friday, up from 4.64% 10 days ago. At one point midweek, the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2008.

Neil Shearing, the chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics , said one impetus for the current wobble had been markets taking a fresh look at the state of US public finances. “There’s been a recalibration,” he said.

Total US government debt has surged past $40tn (£29.5tn), and annual deficits are forecast to be an eye-watering 6% of GDP for the foreseeable future.

Such figures were long deemed barely to matter given the status of US government bonds, or treasuries, as the ultimate safe-haven investment. But as the events that led up to the 2008 financial crisis revealed, things don’t matter in the markets until they do.

“I think we are starting to see a more realistic reassessment of the fiscal pressure in the US,” Shearing said. “What marks the US out is that there’s not really an acknowledgment of the fact that there might be a problem. There’s no plan.”

Russell Jones, a veteran bond market analyst at Llewellyn Consulting, said: “The thing about economics is that often markets delay the judgment and, you know, you can’t really time when they suddenly decide that that’s enough.”

The US treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s recent fumbled attempts to intervene in financial markets – to help Tokyo prop up the yen and then to calm bond yields – have only added to the sense that policymakers are panicking.

Layered on top of these concerns is a more immediate worry about inflation taking off again as a result of renewed hostilities in the Middle East. Oil prices have risen back above $90 a barrel since the US and Iran resumed tit-for-tat attacks.

That has increased expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates – another factor that puts upward pressure on yields.

Every pronouncement by policymakers is being closely scrutinised for clues, including a key speech by the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, last Friday that was read by markets as signalling a willingness to act.

The European Central Bank is expected to lead the charge with a rate rise next week, but markets are telegraphing higher borrowing costs across major economies.

That includes the UK, where investors are now pencilling in three quarter-point rate rises over the next 12 months, and Japan, where the decades-long period of deflation and rock-bottom rates is finally coming to an end.

A dramatic expansion of borrowing by AI “hyperscalers” in the US, to help fund the massive planned expansion of datacentres, has offered investors an alternative home for their cash – and raised questions about the market’s ability to absorb so much debt simultaneously.

Recent calculations by the investment group Vanguard put the value of debt issued by five major tech companies at $135bn (£100bn) this year, up from an average of $35bn between 2020 and 2024.

There is potentially an even more fundamental explanation for an upward shift in borrowing costs, too – based on the growing prevalence of inflationary shocks not just as a result of geopolitical chaos but because of the climate emergency.

Some economists, including the Bank of England policymaker Swati Dhingra, have argued these increasingly regular shocks, as a result of extreme weather events and resulting economic upheaval, could lead to structurally higher interest rates.

Whatever the causes of rising bond yields, the impact is already rippling out worldwide. Public borrowing has increased dramatically in recent years as policymakers have stepped in to cushion consumers against Covid shutdowns, wrestled with sharply higher energy prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and stepped up defence spending. That means small changes in global interest rates can have an outsized impact on government budgets.

In the UK, where £1 in every £12 of public spending already goes on debt interest, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, was pressed this week by the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, about the rising cost of government borrowing.

Higher yields on gilts, as UK government bonds are known, will feed through into predictions of higher interest rate costs for the Treasury ahead of the new chancellor John Healey’s autumn budget.

David Aikman, the director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, urged the government to take the opportunity to implement spending cuts and/or tax increases to help insulate the UK from higher borrowing costs.

“There will be a lot of talk about the fiscal rules. I think that’s slightly missing the point,” he said. “The big point here is we’ve just got a lot of debt, whether you’re missing the rules or not. And it means we’re really vulnerable.”

On the other side of the world, Australian policymakers have been wrestling with similar challenges. Bond yields have breached 15-year highs just days after the country passed A$1tn in government debt.

The timing of the two milestones comes at a difficult time for a Labor government that is under pressure to rein in historically high levels of spending.

Falling house prices in a property-obsessed nation are adding to a mood of discontent. Bets have firmed that the Reserve Bank of Australia could deliver another interest rate hike later this month to tame stubbornly high inflation.

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, has been at pains to highlight Australia’s relatively strong budget position internationally. Australia’s debt is equivalent to about half the size of the economy, which pales against other advanced nations. Similarly, the commonwealth is running deficits, but of less than 1% of GDP.

Chris Richardson, an independent budget expert, said Australia’s government indebtedness wasn’t “bad by world standards”. “But it’s still a lot of debt. And the higher cost of money means the difficult choices that were there already are that much harder.”

For developing countries, these issues are all the more urgent. The International Monetary Fund warned earlier this year that these economies had become more exposed to the risk of higher interest rates, because of the growing importance of lending from short-term investors such as hedge funds, which tend to be more flighty during periods of market volatility.

Matthew Martin, of the advocacy group Development Finance International, said: “A lot of these countries are very near the edge, and if they have to go back to the markets and refinance another bond at 1% or 2% higher than it was before, that will mean even less money to spend on climate action, health and education.”

If higher yields are sustained, the effects will be felt far beyond the world’s treasuries, muddying the maths for corporate investments and putting upward pressure on mortgage rates, which in the UK have already started to rise.

Aikman argued corporate balance sheets worldwide looked less shaky than before the global financial crisis. “We’re not in the place we were in the run-up to 2008,” he said. But he pointed to “pockets” of concern, including the huge scale of debt-fuelled private equity projects that could prove vulnerable in a world of higher rates.

By the end of the week, the sell-off sweeping global bond markets appeared to have eased, for now. But it left yields at levels significantly higher than three months ago – and delivered a painful reminder to policymakers, including Burnham, that in globalised financial markets their plans can be buffeted by forces far beyond their control.

stories.title: Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges
stories.summary: The Reform UK leader promises to deliver on key priorities in the first 100 days of government, if the party wins power.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 minutes ago

Nigel Farage has insisted a Reform UK government would deliver where other parties have failed, as he set out his priorities in his annual conference speech.

He said Reform's pledges for its first 100 days in power would include stopping small boat crossings, cutting energy bills by £250 a year and ending the net zero "lunacy".

To eliminate "obstacles" to his plans, Farage said he would declare a "national emergency" and threatened to overhaul the House of Lords and how judges are appointed if they stood in the way.

In a speech interrupted several times by protesters, the Reform leader was also forced to address allegations over donations which emerged in an undercover investigation.

Reform had been hoping to use its annual conference to regain momentum after a difficult summer dominated by questions over the party's finances.

However, the main day of the conference was overshadowed after two senior party officials stepped down and Reform launched an investigation into claims about funding aired during a Channel 4 News report on Thursday evening, which was filmed by Verbatim Investigations, a group founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting.

Farage insisted "the party has done nothing wrong" and "has taken no illegal money".

He claimed Reform had been "the subject of a highly co-ordinated campaign of attacks" and the allegations had been made "because they're scared of us".

Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' Published 2 hours ago

Farage unveils small boats deal with French National Rally party Published 3 hours ago

Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending Published 1 day ago

In his speech, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader added.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

stories.title: Chinese businesses are giving away AI tokens with coffee, credit cards, and dumplings
stories.summary: Five unexpected ways computing power is entering everyday life in the country.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Innovation

Five unexpected ways computing power is entering everyday life in the country.

Artificial intelligence tokens — once a term familiar only to techies — are rapidly entering everyday life in China.

Banks, cafes, and telcos, among other small and big businesses, are offering free AI tokens as incentives to attract more customers. Some businesses are selling tokens much like mobile data plans, offering them as credit card rewards, or giving them out like free Wi-Fi.

An AI token is essentially a unit of computing that an AI model uses to process text. When a user asks a model a question or gives it an instruction, the words are broken down into small pieces called tokens, which the model processes to generate a response.

500 trillion Daily token consumption in China in mid-2026.

The massive popularity of AI has led to has sharply increase in token consumption globally. Daily token consumption in China surged to 500 trillion in mid-2026 from 100 billion in early 2024.

Token prices have become a new front in the global AI race as U.S. and Chinese AI companies aggressively lower them to compete for wider adoption of their models. Chinese open-source and open-weight models, despite lagging behind U.S. rivals on some measures of frontier performance, can cost 60% to 90% less than comparable models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Cheaper tokens allow Chinese businesses to experiment with ways to package and market them to ordinary consumers.

Poe Zhao, a Beijing-based analyst and founder of the newsletter Hello China Tech , told Rest of World some of the token packages Chinese companies pushed into the consumer market are a “supply-led experiment.”

“Most ordinary users still encounter AI through an app or feature, without seeing a token balance,” he said.

Zhao said China’s effort to bring tokens into the consumer marketplace points to an unusual approach to commercializing AI.

Here are five ways AI tokens are moving into everyday life in China:

AI tokens as credit-card rewards

In July, Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI launched a credit card named after its model Kimi, in partnership with the Agricultural Bank of China and American Express. Users earn Kimi AI tokens, as well as agent and coding quotas, on their spending, just like credit cards reward consumers with airline miles and cashback offers.

The trend began in June, when China Merchants Bank launched a credit card targeting AI developers. It offered new cardholders up to 1.8 billion tokens for use on Chinese AI startup MiniMax’s models.

Shanghai Pudong Development Bank also launched a credit card for AI developers, offering subsidies worth up to 3 billion tokens for Alibaba i Alibaba Alibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall. READ MORE ’s Qwen models.

AI tokens as mobile data

China’s three major telecom operators have packaged AI usage much like mobile data plans.

China Telecom offers consumer plans starting at 9.9 yuan ($1.40) a month for 10 million tokens, with larger allowances available for heavier users and businesses. The company also has a TokenHub platform that offers subscriptions on 142 large models, as the state-owned carrier tries to evolve from selling traditional telecom connectivity to AI computing and services.

Its competitors offer similar plans. China Mobile offered 400,000 tokens for 1 yuan (14 cents) in Shanghai, payable through users’ phone bills. China Unicom introduced monthly plans ranging from 15 yuan ($2.10) for 6 million tokens to 45 yuan ($6.30) for 18 million for business users.

AI tokens as a freebie

Instead of offering free Wi-Fi, an increasing number of Chinese restaurants, cafes, and bars are now luring customers with free AI computing.

At Beijing’s AGI Bar, customers who buy a drink and connect to the Wi-Fi can get unlimited access to DeepSeek V4 Flash. The bar, which targets customers who are programmers and AI startup founders, runs the model locally using a Nvidia DGX Spark workstation.

Nearby, Beijing’s Jingu Yuan dumpling restaurant gives customers 10 yuan ($1.40) worth of computing credits after a meal. Cards on its tables tell diners: “You’re full after eating the dumplings. Go collect some tokens at the cashier so your [AI] agent can be fed with some computing power too.” Its two stores have been handing out more than 100 vouchers a day.

In Changsha, an upcoming 24-hour coffee shop uses a similar approach for promotion, offering customers AI tokens with their coffee.

AI tokens on e-commerce

Tokens have also reached one of China’s largest online secondhand marketplaces . On Alibaba-owned Xianyu, a platform known for selling used phones, furniture, and clothes, sellers advertise cheap access to AI models in packages measured by tokens.

Listings offer millions of tokens for a few dollars in day passes or monthly subscriptions and shared access to AI accounts. Some sellers break up model allowances and resell them to students, independent developers, and small businesses. Others attempt to profit from the gap between official token prices and the discounted or free access they obtained elsewhere.

AI tokens in bank lending

The increasing number of AI startups in China has presented a challenge for its banks, as they struggle to assess the financial status of young companies on traditional metrics such as physical assets.

Banks in the southern city of Guangzhou are experimenting with tokens to boost business for AI startups. The city’s Haizhu district launched a financial product called “token loan” in August. It allows banks including Bank of China, China CITIC Bank, and Bank of Guangzhou to measure a company’s token production and consumption to decide how much it can borrow.

India’s data center boom is leaving the people it displaces with nothing

Communities are being left behind as AI companies secure tax breaks, cheap land from willing governments.

Meta accepts U.S. safety rules while pitching softer tools abroad

As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.

I refused to train the AI that could replace me

AI companies are paying highly educated workers to teach machines the judgment they spent years developing — even when those systems could eventually replace them.

stories.title: Trump’s 100% tariff on drones will be disaster for the US, critics warn
stories.summary: Americans fear there are no cheap alternatives as tariffs suddenly hit drones.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Americans fear there are no cheap alternatives as tariffs suddenly hit drones.

On Thursday, the Trump administration imposed a 100 percent tariff on foreign-made drones, alarming critics who warn that high tariffs would harm public safety and devastate thousands of US businesses.

Guidance posted by US Customs and Border Protection says that starting Thursday, a 100 percent tariff will apply to imported drones that use thermal imaging or weigh more than 55 pounds.

Additionally, a 25 percent tariff has been placed on smaller drones, and drones from US allies were hit with smaller but not inconsequential tariffs. There’s now a 10 percent levy on British-made drones and 15 percent levies on drones from the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan. “Nonsensitive” drones without thermal imaging and their components will carry a 25 percent tariff, starting on February 9, 2027.

While announcing the tariffs, President Donald Trump said that taxing foreign-made drones will strengthen US national security by decreasing reliance on Chinese drones and increasing reliance on domestic drones.

But critics say Trump’s tactics seem short-sighted, citing estimates that “a single Chinese company—Shenzhen-based DJI—manufactures more than 70 percent of the world’s commercial drones,” The New York Times reported .

They fear that Trump’s tariffs will do “more harm than good,” the Times reported, since these drones are considered “essential” for US law enforcement and public safety officials. Thermal drones are regularly used to find missing people, track spreading wildfires, support police and rescue operations in environments with unknown risks, and serve a range of other routine public safety uses. A chief of a large unit comprising police officers and firefighters in the Cleveland area, Scott Mlakar, told the Times that Trump’s tariffs would spike drone costs so much that they would likely “put thermal drones out of reach for communities that needed them the most.”

FCC may effectively ban more drones

Beyond the immediate increase in the cost of drones, even more drones could soon be restricted in the US. The Federal Communications Commission is considering whether to reclassify a range of common drone technologies as “military grade,” a move that many commenters warned would further restrict access to countless drones that serve no military purpose and pose no threat to national security.

Industry experts have warned that the reclassification would amount to a “retroactive ban on drones used by thousands of American businesses and public safety officials,” the Times reported. If passed, it would be an “industry-killing ban,” an aerial photographer, Vic Moss, told the Times. And one official coordinating a city’s drone program, David Hood, urgently alerted the FCC in a comment that the plan to recategorize any drone with Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors as military-grade would be particularly disastrous for society.

“LiDAR is a safety and navigation technology, not a military capability,” Hood wrote. His city relies on LiDAR-equipped aircraft to help avoid crashes. That “civilian use—collision avoidance—is a safety function, not a combat function,” Hood wrote.

He recommended that the FCC either remove LiDAR-equipped drones from the list of potential new categories of military-grade technologies or, at a minimum, narrow the “category so that it reaches only equipment genuinely tied to the identified national-security risk.”

“Prohibiting LiDAR would undermine the very safety the proposal seeks to protect,” Hood wrote. “Removing access to these platforms would push operators—including public agencies conducting inspections and public-safety missions over populated areas—toward less capable aircraft with inferior collision avoidance, increasing the risk of crashes over people and property.”

Dale Hylton of Blue Skies Drones suggested in a comment that the FCC “should evaluate the actual risk presented by a system, not classify equipment as military grade simply because it contains a sensor that is widely used in civilian transportation, robotics, surveying, construction, and industrial applications.”

DJI drones irreplaceable, officials say

Cops in red states like Texas and blue states like New York agree that cutting off Chinese drones will impact public safety.

Jason Lee, a Texas police officer, told the FCC that “there is currently no economically viable domestic replacement” for DJI drones. That’s why, he said, “more than 80 percent of state and local law-enforcement drone programs surveyed in 2024 used DJI aircraft.”

“This widespread adoption did not occur because law-enforcement agencies are seeking military equipment,” Lee said. “It occurred because these systems provide dependable capabilities at a price that municipal agencies can actually afford.”

As the manager of his police department’s drone program, Lee explained that he relies “heavily on DJI platforms because they provide a combination of reliability, capability, ease of use, and cost that is difficult, if not impossible, to replicate with currently available domestic alternatives.”

He’s also concerned that tariffs will make it harder to affordably fix minor repairs on drones that public safety officials have already purchased. Right now, he said, US-made drones can’t fill that gap.

“The fact that a domestic product exists does not necessarily mean it is a viable substitute,” Lee said. “A replacement must be operationally comparable, economically obtainable, supported by an adequate supply chain, and accepted by pilots who must rely on it during real-world incidents.”

Both Lee and Hood noted that the impact extends beyond public safety, affecting hobbyists, professional photographers, farmers, construction workers, and many others who rely on affordable access to capable drones. The American Gas Association, which represents energy groups serving 74 million US residences, noted that it relies on 55-pound drones with thermal imaging and LiDAR to “execute a range of operations common to natural gas utilities, including vegetation management, pipeline inspections, security responses, and disaster recovery.”

The AGA argues that the US should give Americans at least two years to transition from Chinese drones or risk disrupting critical infrastructure.

“A prohibition that eliminates the affordable, capable option without a proven equivalent substitute does not have a minor impact; it strands public agencies with aging fleets and no compliant replacement path, forcing either a loss of capability or substantially higher costs borne by local taxpayers,” Hood said.

Trump urged to expand exemptions

New York State Police officer Michael W. Deyo suggested that the US could establish a pathway to exempt state and local police and public safety agencies from paying tariffs or, at the very least, allow them to apply to import components needed for repairs. Hood similarly requested that the FCC extend exemptions for federal authorities to “state, local, and tribal government operators” that use drones to deliver essential public services.

Mlakar told the Times that Trump’s tariffs appear to be more about “protectionism” than national security. He suggested that lobbying by US manufacturers seeking to eliminate foreign competition was a primary factor in Trump’s decision to impose the tariffs. The Times also noted that Trump’s sons, Eric and Donald Trump Jr., have investments in US drone companies. Both are shareholders and advisory board members of Dominari Holdings, which has invested in Florida-based drone maker Powerus. Don Jr. also sits on the advisory board of Unusual Machines, a top US manufacturer of drone components. On Thursday, Unusual Machines was among the US drone stocks reportedly rallying after the tariffs took effect.

Hood warned that the plan to restrict access to drones with LiDAR sensors would achieve the “opposite” of Trump’s goal to “protect the safety and security of United States persons.”

And the 100 percent tariffs on drones with thermal imaging will likely shift how communities respond to disasters and other scenarios where drones help protect civilians. If public safety officials lose access to DJI drones due to budget constraints, they’ll lose valuable advanced thermal imaging technology that “assist officers and the public in situations where speed, accuracy, and reliable aerial information can directly affect safety,” Lee wrote.

“A thermal-equipped drone can locate a person who cannot otherwise be seen, assist officers searching large or wooded areas, provide information during dangerous incidents, identify heat sources, and support operations where sending an officer into an unknown environment would create unnecessary risk,” he wrote. “These are not military missions. They are routine public-safety applications intended to protect American citizens.”

stories.title: Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk'
stories.summary: Two senior Reform aides have stepped down from their roles following a Channel 4 News and Verbatim film about donations.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has described secretly-recorded comments by his senior aides about donations as "injudicious" and "loose pub talk".

James Orr, the party's head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a close aide to Farage, have both stepped down and Reform has launched an internal investigation into the allegations.

It comes after Channel 4 News broadcast undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations, in which the two men suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

Farage said his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In the Channel 4 report, which aired on Thursday night, a reporter posing as a potential party donor raises a concern to Farage's aide Dan Jukes that his American father wouldn't be able to directly give money to the party within the law.

Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

At the press conference, Farage said that Channel 4 had opted to bleep the names, rather than broadcast them was because Jukes' claims were "simply not true".

He said those donations "haven't occurred" and "don't exist in our accounts".

Farage said his party took compliance around donations "very seriously".

Responding to the allegations, Jukes said: "This was entrapment over a prolonged period of nearly a year by foreign-funded climate change activists.

"I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name."

Before stepping down from his position Jukes had been seen as Farage's right hand man.

Reform's head of policy, James Orr, who also appeared in the film, suggested to the undercover reporter that perhaps his American father could pay for opinion polling to aid Reform's campaigning.

In all, Channel 4 News claims three polls were commissioned in this way costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.

Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.

Orr told Sky News: "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the programme, with which I will cooperate fully."

In response to allegations of "entrapment" from Jukes, a spokesperson for Verbatim Investigations told BBC News the investigation was carried out "to the highest journalistic standards", adding: "As the footage shows, the plots we exposed were proposed by Mr Jukes and Mr Orr, not by our journalists."

Farage acknowledged Jukes' comments were "problematic" but added that they were "loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".

"And whilst I'm aware that our people were pushed and pushed and pushed into saying these things, the comments were injudicious at best.

"Neither of these members were authorised to act in that way.

"Accordingly, they've stepped down pending an investigation, and I emphasise again: Reform has broken no law, and we take compliance around donations very, very seriously."

During the film, Farage is introduced to the undercover reporter posing as a party donor and an actor posing as his American father.

In the press conference, Farage said he was "annoyed" that he was introduced to the two men adding: "It should not have happened."

He said his party needed to "do better as we professionalise".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.

The police said it would assess the matter and any information provided to it.

In a statement on Friday, the Electoral Commission said: "We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police."

A Channel 4 News spokesperson said: "We stand by the public interest journalism in this investigation, which has been rigorously verified to ensure accuracy.

"We would encourage people to watch the investigation in full."

stories.body:
Free AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lesson

A lmost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market . Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.

Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.

This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.

Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.

The market in solar panels was captured. It became the world leader in batteries and electric vehicles . It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.

Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides for failing to boost domestic demand for its products .

Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.

In July, a Chinese startup called Moonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 model and it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.

As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shock might not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power ,” says Campanella.

Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington to antagonise its traditional allies by whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.

The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.

Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI could prick the stock market bubble .

after newsletter promotion

Finally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.

There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.

The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

stories.title: Court Rules Against Citizen Journalists in DMCA Takedown Case—EFF Will Appeal
stories.summary: A federal court in Massachusetts has ruled that copyright holders can issue online takedown notices based on a subjective belief of copyright infringement, even when that belief is unreasonable and self-serving. The case was brought by our client, Channel 781 News, after takedown notices temporarily shut down the citizen journalism group's YouTube channel. We think the court set the bar far too low for copyright takedowns, and we plan to appeal. Channel 781 is a group of independent, volunteer journalists who report on local affairs in Waltham, Massachusetts. That includes posting short, newsworthy excerpts from recordings of city government meetings produced by Waltham Community Access Corporation (WCAC), the city's public access television station. In September 2023, WCAC sent three copyright takedown notices to YouTube targeting fifteen of Channel 781's videos. YouTube removed the videos and, under its three-strikes policy, temporarily disabled Channel 781's entire account—just days before a local election. Represented by EFF and Brown Rudnick LLP, Channel 781 sued WCAC under Section 512(f) of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which provides a remedy when a copyright holder knowingly makes material misrepresentations in a takedown notice. When Is a Copyright Holder Responsible for a Wrongful Takedown? Fair use is the legal right to use copyrighted material without permission, when doing so serves purposes like criticism, commentary, or creating something new. Fair use is not copyright infringement, and courts have recognized that copyright holders must consider fair use before using the DMCA's powerful notice-and-takedown process. In this case, Channel 781 argued that WCAC accused it of copyright infringement without making a good-faith assessment of whether its videos were fair use. The evidence showed that WCAC's analysis was seriously deficient. The court noted that Chris Wangler, the WCAC employee who sent the notices, didn’t consider several facts relevant to fair use. For instance, Channel 781 used relatively small portions of WCAC's recordings, and the underlying recordings were factual public meetings, not a creative work. WCAC also gave little or no weight to whether Channel 781's use harmed any market for the recordings. There’s also strong evidence that WCAC had motivations unrelated to copyright. stories.title: Texas and Florida Step Back from ALPRs
stories.summary: Within the last few days, two important state actions have dealt a big blow to automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks. This is just the latest proof of the growing tide of public opposition to mass surveillance. After years of successful grassroots battles to pull these cameras from local streets, bipartisan momentum is sweeping the country. On August 28, Texas Governor Greg Abbott banned state agencies from spending public funds on Flock cameras . The order dropped just as The Texas Tribune prepared to publish an investigation revealing that a state agency had quietly funneled at least $30 million into building a sprawling surveillance network. Then on August 31, the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) issued a memo , announced by Governor Ron DeSantis, ordering the removal of all ALPRs from the right-of-way on state highways within 30 days. The order revokes all previously approved permits to install ALPRs, and bars transportation officials from issuing future permits. FDOT officials stated that “the recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life.” FDOT’s action has been followed by a surge of local governments in Florida canceling or pausing their vendor contracts . Much more work remains. Many ALPRs in Florida are not on state highways, but sit on city streets, county roads, residential driveways, and shopping center parking lots—and FDOT's order doesn't touch any of them. Likewise, the Texas directive leaves local agencies free to use city, county, federal, and private funds to install cameras. This week’s good news follows years of pushback from local advocates that has seen dozens of cities sever ties with surveillance companies. According to some metrics , during the last 30 days, an average of three localities per day has halted contracts with Flock. Other advocates have been resisting ALPRs in statehouses and court houses , and by blowing the whistle with investigative activism. The moves in Florida and Texas also illustrate the power that the executive branch can wield to curtail mass surveillance with almost immediate results. stories.title: ‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world
stories.summary: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet Since 2009’s Demon’s Souls, Japanese video game director Hidetaka Miyazaki has shown the world a different way to think about game design. His games defy convention with punishing fights, obscure rules, and unknowable, inhospitable worlds. The “Soulslike” genre – named after Demon’s Souls and its sequel Dark Souls – is now ubiquitous, influencing multimillion-sellers from God of War and Star Wars: Jedi to Hollow Knight. Miyazaki’s most recent success, 2022’s Elden Ring , which credited Game of Thrones author George RR Martin as a co-creator, sold over 30m copies and inspired Alex Garland to adapt it for the big screen at A24. It earned Miyazaki a spot on Time magazine’s “most influential” list, an accolade he shares with just one other game developer: Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto. Miyazaki is now 51 and has been FromSoftware’s president since 2014, elevated from game designer to CEO after the success of the Souls series. He has a cherubic face that could pass for 35. He rarely speaks publicly, and never on camera. When he does speak, he answers questions like one of his characters – softly, sadly, his head bowed, making eye-contact only when I am speaking. Outside the studio where we speak is the sprawl of Tokyo’s Shinjuku, an ever-changing maze where tourists get lost and pop-up stores appear and vanish without a trace. Today, a J-pop band performs in the square as the cicadas scream from the trees. A gilded statue of Malania, one of Elden Ring’s toughest bosses, looms over this dimly lit conference room inside From’s headquarters, a bonfire checkpoint away from the chaos. Continue reading...

stories.body:
Bank of England governor says central bankers must explain decisions or risk being seen as ‘unrepresentative elite’

The governor of the Bank of England has said the rise of populist politicians presents a serious challenge to independent central banks.

As Nigel Farage’s Reform UK gathered for its annual conference in Birmingham, Andrew Bailey said central bankers must be prepared to explain their decisions to the public or risk being attacked as an “unrepresentative elite”.

Bailey was speaking at a conference at the London School of Economics . In an address peppered with historical references, from Alexander Hamilton to Thomas Hobbes, he said central banks must not take their “legitimacy for granted”.

Bailey said populist parties’ pitch for power “often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people. Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty.”

He added: “This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it.”

Populist parties, especially of the right, have been riding high on both sides of the Atlantic in recent years. Attacking traditional institutions – including central banks – often forms part of their platform.

Farage has previously suggested he would like to replace Bailey if Reform comes to power. In the US, Donald Trump repeatedly launched tirades against the former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell over the central bank’s failure to cut interest rates.

Bailey was among the international central bankers who signed a joint statement defending Powell against Trump’s criticism and stressing the importance of independence.

The Bank of England was made independent by the Labour government in 1997, handing decisions on interest rates from the chancellor to a nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) chaired by the governor.

After the 2008 global financial crisis, which led to a significant proportion of the UK banking sector being nationalised at taxpayer expense, the Bank of England was given additional responsibilities for financial stability.

Bailey said on Friday that insulating the Bank from politics had made it better able to fulfil its role of maintaining “the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible”.

He said: “Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.”

after newsletter promotion

The MPC is split over how to respond to rising inflation as a result of the Iran war. Bailey has stressed that in a weak jobs market, he does not yet see signs of the “second-round effects” that can embed inflation throughout the economy as workers bid up their wages to keep pace.

The MPC voted to keep interest rates on hold at 3.75% at its last meeting in July. But three members voted for a rate rise, including the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, Huw Pill, who used a speech on Thursday to reiterate that in the face of rising inflation, Threadneedle Street should act “clearly, promptly and decisively”.

At its next policy meeting on 17 September, the Bank is also expected to announce whether it will press ahead with its controversial policy of quantitative tightening. The Bank has been progressively selling off the bonds it acquired though the emergency policy of quantitative easing – creating money to help stave off recession.

Critics, from Reform to leftwing thinktanks, have argued that these sales tend to drive up the yield, or interest rate, on government bonds, which move in the opposite direction to prices. That makes it more expensive for the government to borrow, a pressing issue at a time of febrile bond markets .

Bailey will appear before MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee next week to explain his thinking.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 September 2026, 03:01 BST

Argentina's president has heightened tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands, warning he will impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil close to the British overseas territory.

In a national address, Javier Milei said the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands, emboldened by signs the US might reconsider its stance of neutrality on the issue.

Milei said the Sea Lion oilfield, where a British and an Israeli firm are due to begin exploration work, was a "clear and present danger".

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK's position on the islands was "unwavering", and they would remain British as "that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders."

Trump hints US would not back UK over Falkland Islands due to lack of Iran war support Published 1 day ago

Falklands is a pressure point for the UK – and the US knows it Published 24 April

Earlier Downing Street said reaffirmed its position that the islands would remain a British Overseas Territory "for as long as the Islanders wish".

"This is not the first time Argentine governments have made economic threats against the islanders. We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources."

More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.

Milei announced his sanctions plan surrounded by his cabinet at the presidential palace, reiterating that the Falklands were "historically and legally" Argentinean.

It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he said on X.

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

Teslyn Barkman, a former member of the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, told the BBC that Milei's speech had "probably irked every single Falkland islander".

Speaking from the capital Stanley, she added that "we have a burgeoning economy for a small place... we will remain forever British".

The crux was a proposal to introduce a bill to parliament to impose sanctions on energy firms planning to begin oil exploration off the Falklands.

The Sea Lion oilfield , around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil .

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

Rockhopper has described the field as containing "highly marketable crude".

In a video posted earlier this year, Navitas highlighted the work it is already carrying out in the Falklands including building a dock, a heliport and accommodation for oil workers.

In a statement, Rockhopper and Navitas said the two firms believed that "the recent developments are not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development".

Milei said "If we do not act swiftly in a few months, they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before," Milei said.

There is both a domestic and a regional political dimension to this latest escalation on the Falklands.

At home, Milei needs to shore up votes amid his plummeting popularity, currently languishing at around 34%. There is only a year to go before he faces a presidential election and a serious challenge from his erstwhile vice-president, Victoria Villarruel.

A pro-military politician, she has criticised his diplomatic efforts to secure change on the question of Falklands sovereignty. The sanctions may be part of a wider attempt to stave off accusations that he's weak on an issue which is so fundamental to Argentine identity.

It helps Milei that this is about something concrete – the impending oil exploration of an oilfield rather than broad questions of sovereignty and self-determination. He argues that the UK is acting in violation of a UN resolution urging the two sides not to take unilateral action while the dispute remains unresolved.

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said , describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

"There are winds of change in the world that are favourable to our claim," Milei added.

When asked in an interview with GB News earlier on Thursday if the US would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump replied that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review .

Hours before Milei's speech, Sarah Rogers, a senior official in the US state department, posted a photo of herself with Milei alongside the caption: "Exciting things are happening in the Western Hemisphere."

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

stories.body:
Reform UK’s national conference has been rocked by allegations that senior members of the party plotted to circumvent rules on political donations. The reports centre on two payments – one real and one suggested, but both important. The two Reform staff members at the centre of the investigation have been suspended.

The apparent plans were captured in a sting, filmed in London and Clacton by undercover journalists from Verbatim Investigations and broadcast by Channel 4 News. The first allegation from the film is that James Orr, who was Reform’s head of policy until his suspension, arranged for an impermissible donor to pay for £32,500 of polling , which later made headlines in national newspapers, from the company JL Partners.

The question surrounding the payment is whether it is allowed under electoral law, and whether it should have been reported to the Electoral Commission .

The law is clear that if you pay for research on behalf of a party (this is known as sponsorship ), that payment counts as a donation and ought to be recorded as such. So, there is a question about why this donation does not appear in the Electoral Commission database.

However, a more pertinent issue is one of permissibility – basically, who is legally allowed to give money in UK politics. A person or company from the US, say, is categorically not a permissible source. If a UK party receives a donation from an impermissible source, it must be returned .

This will be a matter for the Electoral Commission to decide on. However, it is an offence under electoral law to attempt to evade permissibility restrictions on donations, or “participate in an arrangement or withhold information” about them.

Reform UK has been reported to the police and the party has launched an internal probe. But it has denied wrongdoing and says it was the target of a hoax.

Farage on film

Even more damaging for party leader Nigel Farage (because he was filmed discussing it) may be the promise of £500,000 from a – fictional – American businessman. This donation appeared to be offered to be funnelled through the businessman’s British-born son. Farage can be heard on the film thanking the undercover reporters, who are posing as the father and son.

There was also footage of Farage’s then-aide Dan Jukes (now suspended), who appears to be discussing previous examples of this kind of arrangement. In the film, a series of bleeps can be heard – possibly as Jukes is naming names.

There is a third question, which concerns the effect the polling had – its “bang for buck” , as Farage put it.

In electoral terms, £32,500 is a piddling sum, less than 0.05% of the total spent by all political parties at the 2024 UK general election. But it may still have had a significant impact.

These polls were covered on the front pages of national newspapers, showing just how far a little bit of money can go. They were stories that added to the wider narrative of a surge in Reform’s popularity.

There is nothing new about this. Once, having too much time on my hands, I dug around the Electoral Commission political finance database trying to work out how much the infamous Brexit bus had cost, and found it was about £90,000.

I imagine this is one of the main things the UK public remembers about that campaign. The point is a well-placed message , playing into pre-existing narratives, can be priceless.

But there is also a wider point, which I have made to parliamentary committees . In an increasingly fragmented political environment, money matters far more than it once did – and goes much further.

In the UK’s traditional two-party system, there was a smaller persuadable electorate, and therefore money had diminishing returns. But now the margins are thinner, and elections can be won on 30% or less of the vote. Not only does every penny count, but every penny goes further.

If, with polling evidence, you can play into the narrative that Reform is now the party to beat on the right, for example, that can act as rocket fuel – not just for Reform’s true believers, but wavering Tories.

Read more: Why the questions about Reform UK and its wealthy donors won’t go away

Polling matters, because it changes minds and influences the political strategies that decide elections. James Johnson, founding director of JL Partners, is seen on the undercover film discussing the company’s “informal rule bending” . These polls would not have been front-page news if the Reform connection had been known.

JL Partners has serious questions to answer about its operating practices in the wake of these revelations. The company has accepted it breached British Polling Council rules, saying it contacted the body after becoming aware and pledging an internal review of its processes.

This story also reminds us that questions about party funding are not going away. We know that British politics has well and truly entered the era of the mega-donor , and we know that the public don’t like it .

Despite setting up a cross-government taskforce , Labour could have moved faster to apply a universal cap on donations . This story reminds us there is an urgent need to reflect on how to address the access and influence that money has on UK democracy.

Whether to grasp this particular nettle will be one of the key issues that defines this government. The Representation of the People Bill is moving through parliament. But anyone who has seen the undercover footage may feel that the ban on cryptocurrency donations and £100,000 limit on donations from voters based abroad that it proposes won’t be enough to fix things.

If this doesn’t inspire Labour’s new taskforce to be bold in seeking solutions that every party can get behind, what will?
