stories.body:
Party podcast and social media host Ray Addison fronted films about province where China is accused of genocide

Reform UK’s top media presenter has worked for a Chinese state propaganda channel within the past year, the Guardian can reveal.

Ray Addison, who presents the political party’s in-house podcast and social media campaigns, fronted films about Xinjiang province – where the Chinese government is accused of committing genocide – for state media in September 2025.

In the videos, entitled Raymond’s Xinjiang Stories, some of which praise Chinese infrastructure, Addison described himself as a CGTN correspondent. The series was made after Addison left GB News in 2024, where he had worked as a news presenter and reporter.

Xinjiang province has attracted international attention because of alleged human rights abuses against the region’s Muslim Uyghur population by the Chinese state, including claims of forced labour, sterilisation, re-education and mass surveillance.

Addison’s work for China contrasts with the hard line Reform has taken on Chinese issues ranging from industrial relations to suspected Chinese state espionage within Westminster.

In a social media video posted by GB News in January, Nigel Farage said of the UK’s relationship with China: “I’m very, very nervous about the extent to which China has effectively spied on us, stolen many of our industrial secrets. I’m worried about the extent to which they’ve infiltrated, using money, British universities. We must be cautious about the relationship.”

The videos presented by Addison for CGTN are publicly available on YouTube and carry a warning stating that “CGTN is funded in whole or in part by the Chinese government”.

CGTN lost its licence to broadcast in the UK in 2021 after the regulator Ofcom determined it was ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party.

US goverments under both the previous Trump and Biden administrations have formally described China’s actions against the Uyghurs and other ethnic groups in the province as genocide . The UK government has not made a formal declaration but has noted concerns about alleged human rights abuses in the region. In 2021, British MPs voted to declare that China is committing genocide against the Uyghur people in Xinjiang.

Suella Braverman, now a Reform MP, has also made public statements to this effect. On 14 January 2025, before she defected from the Conservative party to Reform, she posted on X: “China is committing genocide in Xinjiang, funding Putin’s war of aggression in Europe and has committed acts of cyber-terrorism against the British people.”

Addison is paid by Reform to produce content about the party and creates social media videos as well as presenting its The Reform UK Podcast. In recent days he has fronted the party’s social media promotion of its conference, which is being held in Birmingham.

The party has sought to capitalise on Farage’s fanbase by advertising its podcast on the basis of exclusive interviews with the party leader and other senior party figures.

Several countries have banned or limited imports of Chinese cotton from Xinjiang because of allegations that the regime uses Uyghur slave labour to process the material.

after newsletter promotion

In one video posted on YouTube in September 2025, which appears to be filmed in Xinjiang, Addison describes the “gorgeous [cotton] fields all around me” and in solely favourable terms describes how technology is being used to boost cotton yields. He adds: “Xinjiang’s cotton story is no longer just about scale, it’s about transformation.”

Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, has said the party was concerned about a range of behaviour by the Chinese Communist party, including its threat to Taiwan.

“We are very anxious about multiple areas of what China is doing, and I think we need to be much stricter on it,” he told a podcast last year. Tice went on to say that the last Conservative government had been “too permissive” of China and called for the west to make it clear to China it would “come down like a ton of bricks” both militarily and economically.

Iain Duncan Smith, one of a number of British MPs and peers targeted by Chinese sanctions, criticised Reform’s engagement of Addison. “There is a question of what due diligence will have been carried out. Everything in China is controlled by the state and if you have someone who has been employed by state media then that means they will have been employed by the state,” he said.

Reform was aware of Addison’s work for a Chinese government-controlled media outlet before he was appointed. A spokesperson did not answer specific questions about its vetting process.

A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK stands by its critical comments regarding China. Ray has worked for a number of British media outlets such as GB News. He has had a successful career in journalism all over the world. Ray Addison has never tried to hide where he has worked, it’s all over the internet and easily found with a Google search.”

stories.summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber. stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border

After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.

Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.

At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”

“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet , which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.

According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

stories.title: Three crucial questions facing Farage at Reform conference
stories.summary: Can the Reform UK leader put his policies into action, and become prime minister?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 September 2026, 06:00 BST

More than 30 years after he first stood for Parliament, Nigel Farage seems to be approaching the climax of his long, storied, and controversial career.

The big unknown: can the 62-year-old put his radical policies into practice by becoming prime minister?

The latest revelations about the party's apparent attitude to donations have ended up dragging Reform into another cycle of bad headlines.

Arguably how it plays out depends on the answers to three central questions.

Will allegations about cash permanently damage Farage?

The Reform leader is already facing investigations into his own finances and those of his party, and concerns about his friendship with a convicted fraudster.

And now there is the possibility of yet more inquiries after an undercover sting which targeted Reform's handling of wealthy donors.

An investigation, filmed by Verbatim Investigations and broadcast by Channel 4 News, shows a senior Farage aide suggesting a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000 for the party.

Reform denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".

Meanwhile Farage's personal popularity already seems to be slightly on the slide and before news of the investigation broke, I spoke to commentators about the party's prospects.

"Among true believers Nigel Farage's personal ratings remain as strong as ever," says Luke Tryl from pollsters More in Common.

"But among the wider public he's taken a dip from being the party leader with the highest net approval this time last year, to being close to tying [Green Party leader Zack] Polanski at the bottom of the pack today".

The barrage of questions about finances prompted the Reform leader to quit Parliament and call the Clacton by-election but his resounding victory in that contest last month has not quietened his critics.

Even some on Farage's own side believe the stresses of the summer have changed the Reform leader's mood during public appearances.

"Why has Nigel, the most successful politician across 25 years, changed from the man who people want to have a drink with?" asks Tim Montgomerie, the Tory defector who was recently suspended from Reform for criticising senior figures.

"He's looked miserable, defensive, and complaining. He needs to get over it, and I think we'll see a better, more attractive Nigel in the coming days."

Farage's biographer, the veteran political journalist Michael Crick, has also noticed a shift.

"You've seen a much more aggressive Farage in the last three or four months. He's gone from the affable to the laughable," says Crick. "That's not going to appeal to waverers, or to moderate conservatives who might be thinking about defecting."

Crick is one of at least eight journalists to have been banned from Reform's conference. Many of them have uncovered uncomfortable details about the party's finances.

In response, Reform says that they have granted accreditation to at least 1,000 members of the media.

Can Reform maintain momentum?

The party's 15 months of consistently leading opinion polls are now over.

That is partly due to a resurgent Labour Party under Andy Burnham, and the rise of Restore, a party led by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

But regular headlines about party finances, plus the ongoing parliamentary investigation into Farage's decision not to register the £5m "unconditional gift" he received from a billionaire, could also be changing voters' minds.

"People still think Britain isn't working," says Tryl. "And the populist right is doing well in pretty much every European country. But the £5m gift, Nigel Farage's friendship with Donald Trump, and the [US] president's war in Iran have prompted some concerns about Reform".

The party's strategy is to fight back, talk up the likelihood of a snap election next spring and unveil plans for their first 100 days in government. This includes a relentless onslaught of new policies from housing, to the economy and immigration.

"We are in an attention economy and the moment you stop swimming, you die," says one party strategist. "We need to keep it up."

The appearance at the conference today of France's 30-year-old right-wing star Jordan Bardella, is an attempt to show off the international links Farage has fostered. Bardella could be France's prime minister if his colleague Marine Le Pen wins the presidency

In the coming weeks Reform plan to unveil more members of their "shadow cabinet". Insiders say their new recruits will be experienced, talented figures from outside politics. "You'll be impressed. I promise," says one involved.

Yet Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has also refreshed her top team and is showing signs of successfully rebuilding her party's reputation.

"The big risk for Reform is if the Tories pull ahead consistently," says Tryl. "There is a chunk of Tory-Reform waverers who only care about beating Labour, and they will vote for whoever is in the lead in the polls."

"Burnham is a more formidable opponent," concedes Tim Montgomerie. "But however much charisma and vibe the PM has, reality will soon catch up with him."

Farage attends the business day of Reform UK's annual conference at the NEC in Birmingham

Is the party really professionalising?

"There aren't going to be any singalongs at conference this year," says a Reform aide. "Or any COVID deniers."

At last year's event, regional mayor Andrea Jenkyns sang a self-penned rock song on stage, and a guest speaker claimed that Covid vaccines were linked to the cancers of King Charles III and the Princess of Wales. This time, the party is hoping to project a far more serious image.

Farage has also finally surmounted many of the internal problems that bedevilled his previous parties. Ukip in particular had significant struggles with money, resources and organisation.

In contrast, Reform UK has oodles of cash thanks to the generosity of crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. The party recently received another £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto billionaire.

The party has in just two years built a slick press, marketing and social media operation.

But insiders say there are still problems with candidate selection and polling, and Farage's loyalty to long-term aides is partly to blame.

"There are too many staff who Nigel's had for too long, who he is loyal to, but who won't take Reform from where they are to where they need to be," says Montgomerie.

"The quality of Reform opinion polling is nowhere near as good as the Tories are getting. They never know what's going on at the ground level. Their intelligence at the last three by-elections has been way off."

The aggressive style of the party's home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf, has also led to internal friction.

Yusuf is credited with professionalising the party and is hugely popular with Reform members, but not with all of his colleagues. Last month he called former Tory Defence Secretary Ben Wallace a "traitor to Britain" and was reprimanded by Farage.

"Zia's a valued colleague," says one party insider with a grin. Others are more blunt and believe the current situation is unsustainable. "You can't keep blowing stuff up. You can't keep on massacring your own side," says one senior Farage ally. "Nigel is loyal but he's also pragmatic."

Reform may have had a difficult few months, yet they have maintained a big base of supporters.

"It's easy to think they are finished and on the way out," says Crick.

"But to have more than 20% in the opinion polls is way beyond what they got at the election, and it's a very good base to build from".

Whether or not Burnham calls a snap general election next spring, Farage is in the best position of his life to get hold of real power.

This weekend's conference, and how Farage responds to the latest allegations about his colleagues, should give us a strong sign as to whether he is ruthless and focussed enough to achieve it.

stories.body:
The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election

T o outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’s downfall . Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it was electoral threats from Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.

Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.

In that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop her aping his stances ). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.

This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.

The claim to be the true keeper of the Thatcherite flame has become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “ mini-budget ” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.

One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, was this week appointed Mrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.

This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.

stories.body:
US job report smashes forecasts

Newsflash: Hiring has surged across the US economy.

Employment surged by 162,00 in August, much stronger than the 56,000 new hires expected, the latest non-farm payroll report shows.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that employment increased in food services and drinking places and in local government education, while the information industry lost jobs.

And in another important development – the US did not shed jobs in July, as first reported.

The BLS reports that there were 44,000 more jobs than it previously estimated in July – meaning employment rose by 21,000, rather than falling by 23,000.

The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for June was revised up by 11,000, from +20,000 to +31,000, too.

This should cheer the Trump White House.

But it might cause some on the Federal Reserve to ponder whether the labor market might be strong enough to handle higher interest rates….

Closing post

That’s all for another week…

The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market.

The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November, according to new data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Despite the relative stability of the unemployment rate, the number of new jobs added to the economy has been fluctuating, going from 214,000 in March down to a 21,000 gain in July and then back up in August.

Shares in companies seeking oil off the Falklands Islands have fallen , after Argentina threatened sanctions. Rockhopper shares have closed down 6.4% tonight, with Border & Southern shedding 12.6%.

Global food prices have hit a three-year high.

The governor of the Bank of England has said the rise of populist politicians presents a serious challenge to independent central banks.

As Nigel Farage’s Reform UK gathered for its annual conference in Birmingham, Andrew Bailey said central bankers must be prepared to explain their decisions to the public or risk being attacked as an “unrepresentative elite”.

The car company Volkswagen has approved controversial plans to shed 100,000 jobs in a battle for survival as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals.

And the slump in UK housebuilding has continued…

After a quiet day’s trading, the London market has closed broadly where it began the session!

The FTSE 100 share index has closed down 0.4 of a point at 10,831 points.

IT services company Computacenter (+45) led the risers, followed by DIY chain Kingfisher (+3.2%)

UK government bonds have had a calm day too – prices have strengthened a little, pushing down the yields on 10 and 30-year gilts.

A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea has proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher.

More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as the conflict has intensified , making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in the strait of Hormuz , Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası.

Trump: Fed must cut rates

Donald Trump has urged the US Federal Reserve to cut US interest rates, in a Truth Social post bragging about today’s strong jobs figures.

The president posted:

double quotation mark Great jobs number just announced, breaking all estimates (except mine!) by double and triple - And you haven’t seen anything yet! EMPLOYERS ADDED 162,000 JOB IN AUGUST. Lower the interest rates because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago! A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE - IT’S A BETTER CREDIT…Very simple! We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like “the old days.” Without the United States agreeing to allow them their big surpluses, and we could stop that immediately, they would no longer be considered financially ELITE! LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT, which the U.S. Supreme Court, in its ridiculous and very costly Tariff decision, strongly acknowledged “the President” has an absolute right to do. IT’S BETTER THAN TARIFFS! The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen! President DONALD J. TRUMP

However, the Fed’s ‘great new leader’, Kevin Warsh, is more concerned that inflationary pressures are building, which might prompt him to vote for a rate rise not a cut.

Canada’s jobs market stumbled in August.

While the US added jobs, Canada shed 41,700 positions in August, data showed on Friday. This included a 19,000 drop in employment among young people, aged 15 to 24.

That follows an unusually strong summer hiring, though.

Some stocks have dropped at the start of trading in New York, in the latest sign that good economic news can be bad for markets.

The Dow Jones industrial average responded to the better-than-expected jobs report by dropping 169 points, or 0.3%, to 53,516 points.

The broader S&P 500 index is down almost 0.1%.

Today’s August jobs report “shocked everybody”, says Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, explaining:

double quotation mark The economy added 162,000 jobs, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1%. In a normal world, that is good news. Employers hired. The labor market did not roll over. Markets, of course, are not living in a normal world. When it comes to interest rates, bad news has been good news and good news has been a problem. A strong payroll number keeps alive the chance the Federal Reserve tightens again. Futures had already been pricing a higher chance of a September rate hike. A 162,000 print — well above the roughly 56,000 economists expected, and far above the 31,000 average monthly gain over the prior year — does not make that debate go away.

US government bond yields have risen, as the strong jobs report reignites bets on early interest rate rises.

The moves aren’t huge, though. The yield, or interest rates on 10-year US treasury bonds is up 3 basis points (0.03 of a percentage point) to 4.792%.

Shorter-dated debt (which is more sensitive to rate expectations) has moved more sharply. Two-year US Treasury yields are up 7 basis points to 4.406%, and Reuters reports they also hit their highest since January 2025.

Here’s Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot , with some rapid reaction to the US jobs report:

double quotation mark “Today’s US nonfarm payrolls report was an important test of whether July’s surprise decline in employment was the beginning of something more troubling, but with 162,000 jobs added in August, the unemployment rate holding steady at 4.1%, and July’s figure revised up to an increase of 21,000, it seems there was no need to worry. “The figures should offer some reassurance to Federal Reserve policymakers ahead of the meeting later this month, as a swift return to job growth supports the view that the labour market has managed to remain broadly stable despite the loss of momentum seen in recent months. Key drivers of this uplift were increases in food services and drinking places, as well as in local government education. Meanwhile, the information industry saw a decline.”

The dollar is rallying

Today’s forecast-smashing US jobs report has given the US dollar a lift.

The dollar index (which tracks the greenback against a basket of other currencies), is up 0.4%, gaining against the pound and the euro.

Where the US economy added, or lost, jobs in August

Here are highlights from today’s US labor market report:

Employment in food services and drinking places increased by 59,000 in August.

Local government education added 42,000 jobs in August

Employment in manufacturing continued its upward trend, rising by 16,000

Employment in health care continued to trend up, by 13,000

But…

Information employment declined by 23,000 in August, following losses that had averaged 8,000 per month over the prior 12 months. In August, job losses occurred in computing infrastructure providers, data processing, web hosting, and related services (-8,000), in publishing industries (-7,000), and in broadcasting and content providers (-5,000).

stories.body:
UK bond yields drop at start of trading

The UK government bond market is open! And there is reassuring news for borrowers, and our political leaders.

UK bond prices are strengthening, a little, which is pushing down the yield (or rate of return) on these gilts.

10-year UK bond yields have dropped by over 4 basis points (0.04 of a percentage point) to 5.195%, away from the 18-year high set yesterday.

30-year bond yields are down 4bps too, to 5.831%.

Update: AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould reports there is “a measure of calm in government bond markets” today, as the oil price drops.

With Brent crude down about 0.5% at $95.20 a barrel, some of the fears of an inflationary shock that would drive interest rates higher may be easing.

Closing post

Time to wrap up…

Some calm has returned to markets today, after recent turbulence in the bond markets.

UK government debt has recovered some of its recent losses, which has pushed down borrowing costs. The yield, or rate of return, on UK 10-year debt is now down 10 basis points (0.1 of a percentage point) at 5.13%, away from the 18-year high set yesterday.

US central banker Christopher Waller helped to calm investors’ worries by saying he is leaning towards holding US interest rates unchanged at this month’s meeting.

However, the Bank of England’s chief economist, Huw Pill , is pushing for a rise in UK borrowing costs.

Mortgages are already expected to rise, due to the recent jump in UK bond yields.

AJ Bell head of financial analysis Danni Hewson sums up the day:

double quotation mark “It’s been a brighter day for global markets as bond yields stabilised and comments from Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller took some heat out of rate hike expectations. “Whilst the price of Brent crude jumped to nearly to $97 a barrel as tensions in the Middle East continue to simmer, Mr Waller saying he could argue in favour of keeping the US base rate at its current level to give prices a chance to cool off helped lift market sentiment. A slightly higher than expected unemployment count added more weight to the scale, but August’s inflation data will be the ultimate test next week.

Here’s today’s stories:

Bitcoin back over $80,000

Back in the financial markets, bitcoin has hit a four-month high.

The crypto asset has jumped back over the $80,000 mark to trade as high as $81,383 this afternoon.

Simon Peters , crypto analyst at etoro , explains why:

double quotation mark Recent moves from the US Treasury - that it will double the size of its long-dated bond buybacks and a willingness to use the General Account to support the long end of the bond market - has brought liquidity back into focus, and in turn renewed interest in bitcoin, as historically it has been a key beneficiary of increased market liquidity. Attention also remains on the Federal Reserve, which controls short-term interest rates. While inflation remains above target, any signs of a meaningful cooling of inflation over the coming months could provide a further tailwind for bitcoin by increasing the prospect of a more accommodative monetary policy. Going into the last months of 2026, seasonality could also play a role. The fourth quarter has historically been bitcoin’s strongest performing quarter of the year.

In his speech, Huw Pill also argues that the Bank cannot sit on its hands just because the financial markets have tightened financial conditions because they expect rate hikes .

That tightening (the City expects three rate hikes by the end of next year) has, arguably, done some of the Bank’s job for it.

Pill , though, explains that this situation could backfire though:

double quotation mark While we can continue for a while under the assumption that markets ‘have done our job for us’ by repricing the short-end following the energy price shock, when those market expectations depart from an unchanged path for Bank Rate (as they do at the time of writing), at some point we will unavoidably face the choice of validating the forward rate curve (by hiking Bank Rate) or acquiescing in the curve shifting downward (by continuing to hold Bank Rate). There is no free lunch. And the danger exists that the market may lose confidence that expected Bank Rate increases will be implemented just at the time as it starts to entertain doubts that the MPC ability or willingness to bring inflation down to target. Indeed, one would expect that to be the case. So, there is potential ‘wrong-way risk’ here: in this setting, the market will ease financial conditions just when the MPC needs them to tighten.

BoE chief economist pushes for interest rate rise

The Bank of England’s chief economist is to renew his push for an increase in UK interest rates today.

Huw Pill will tell the Edinburgh Chamber of Commerce that “clear, prompt and decisive policy action and communication” would help to avoid the danger that inflationary pressures from the Iran war become embedded and persistent.

Pill , who was part of the minority of policymakers who voted for a rate rise in July, argues that “acting clearly, promptly and decisively with Bank Rate” would be effective at dampening down inflation pressures.

Pill will say:

double quotation mark At a time of profound uncertainty, it is important that the MPC offers an anchor for the short end of the market curve, rather than gives the impression that it is chasing market expectations. As reflected in my vote in recent policy rounds, I see benefit in acting clearly, promptly and decisively with Bank Rate. This would cut through the noise inherent in the current uncertain environment in a way that bolsters the clarity and effectiveness of our policy choices.

Key components for UK's first small nuclear reactor to be built in Newcastle

Siemens Energy’s Newcastle site has won an important contract in the energy world today – to make steam turbine components for Rolls-Royce SMR’s first three small modular reactors.

Those SMRs are being built on Anglesey in North Wales , and Siemens Energy is to become the first company to manufacture components – including high-pressure turbines and valve casings – for a small modular reactor anywhere in Europe.

Miatta Fahnbulleh , secretary of state for energy security and net zero, says:

double quotation mark This is what our golden age of nuclear looks like in practice: skilled jobs in Newcastle, stronger British manufacturing and a more secure energy future. Producing these components here in the UK will help strengthen our energy security, reduce our exposure to volatile international gas markets, create new export opportunities for British industry, and reindustrialise the UK.

Back in April, Rolls-Royce secured up to £599m from Britain’s national wealth fund to help it in the race to develop the UK’s first small modular nuclear reactors at Wylfa, Anglesey.

Wall Street opened higher on relief that Federal Reserve policymaker Chris Waller isn’t learning towards voting for a rate hike ( see last post ).

The Dow Jones industrial average has gained 363 points, or 0.7%, to 53,425, with the broader S&P 500 index up 0.5%.

Fed's Waller indicates he will support holding rates steady at September meeting

Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller has said today he is leaning toward keeping interest rates steady at the central bank’s September meeting, provided there are no surprises from upcoming inflation data.

In an interview with Reuters, Waller expressed confidence in the current inflation trends – just days after Fed chair Kevin Warsh argued that there could be ‘work to do’ to tackle inflation.

Waller said:

double quotation mark I’m going to paraphrase John Lennon here. Give disinflation a chance. I’m not going to say let’s wait until next year, but let’s just wait and see if we get some improvement on this.”

These comments seem to be pushing the dollar down, adding to the yen’s rise today – Japan’s currency has now gained almost 2% today.

Nvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face is another sign (see earlier post) that the company’s ambitions extend far beyond selling chips.

Axel Rudolph , chief technical analyst at investing and trading platform IG, explains:

double quotation mark By bringing one of the key platforms for open-source and open-weight AI models into its ecosystem, Nvidia gains a much deeper relationship with developers and a new route into the software and deployment layers of AI. The deal could help sustain demand for Nvidia hardware while reducing its reliance on a handful of hyperscalers, but there is a clear risk that Hugging Face’s appeal as a neutral platform could be weakened if developers fear Nvidia is taking too much control. The price tag looks hefty on conventional measures, but Nvidia is clearly buying strategic influence as much as current earnings. And despite the scale of the deal, there still looks to be plenty of mileage left in the Nvidia share price: the company is expanding into more parts of the AI ecosystem, while its valuation does not look excessive when viewed against its longer-term growth prospects.”

New claims for unemployment support in the US have risen slightly.

There were 206,000 fresh ‘initial claims’ for jobless support last week, a rise of 2,000, new data from the US department of labor shows.

Nvidia to buy Hugging Face for $13bn

Newsflash: Nvidia has agreed to buy AI model platform Hugging Face for $13bn.

Hugging Face is a database of AI models, which recently hit the headlines after being hacked by a rogue group of OpenAI’s agents.

Announcing the deal, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang says Hugging Face is “a vibrant home for the open model developer community”.

Huang says that the deal will speed up the spread of open models, and pledges to help scale up Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions.

Huang explains:

double quotation mark More than 18 million developers, researchers and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3m models, 500,000 datasets and 1m applications. More than 200,000 companies use the platform to discover, evaluate, customize and deploy AI. Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem. Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want. Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

UK government bonds are continuing to rally, pushing down borrowing costs.

With prices rising, the yield on 10-year gilts is now down over 6 basis points (0.06 of a percentage point) to 5.176%. That wipes out all Wednesday’s rise, and some of Tuesday’s too.

Oil has shaken off its earlier losses, and is pushing higher as traders fret about the Middle East conflict.

Israeli defense minister Israel Katz has warned that if Iran attacks Israel, the military will target all of the regime’s infrastructure, “including energy infrastructure.”

Speaking at a Jewish New Year toast with Defense Ministry employees, Katz said:

double quotation mark There are signs we are seeing that indicate that the heavy economic pressure Iran is under and the fear of an uprising and the fall of the regime could push them to desperate measures. An Iranian attack on Israel will free us from all constraints. We will strike all infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and return Iran to the Stone Age and darkness.

Joe Maher , markets economist at Capital Economics , has predicted that UK government bonds will recover over the coming months, pushing down yields.

He told clients:

double quotation mark Higher energy prices alongside renewed fiscal concerns have pushed Gilt yields to multi-decade highs, but we continue to think they will fall back over the next year or so.

US layoffs slow despite AI

Over in the US, the pace of job cuts have slowed despite firms using AI to cut their workforces.

Coaching company Challenger, Gray & Christmas have calculated that US-based employers announced 33,429 job cuts in July, down 27% compared with June, and nearly half as many as in July 2025.

It’s the lowest monthly total in two years.

Andy Challenger , workplace expert and chief revenue officer for Challenger, Gray & Christmas, explains:

double quotation mark “The pace of layoffs fell dramatically this summer. Layoff plans continue to be announced primarily in Tech, and artificial intelligence is still the story, as investments in the technology reshape organizations. “Hiring has also increased over last year by 25%, so while AI is shifting the labor market, it is not dismantling it.

But….

Technology companies announced 9,867 job cuts in July, taking the total so far this year up to 149,023.

Challenger says:

double quotation mark “Tech remains the center of gravity for this year’s cuts, and AI is still the reason companies give.”

Upmarket cinema chain Everyman saw revenues surge by a quarter and admissions rise by a fifth in the first half of the year, as blockbusters including the Michael Jackson music biopic and The Devil Wears Prada sequel saw box office sales top £600m in the UK & Ireland for the first time since before the pandemic.

Everyman , which is in the process of being taken private by its biggest shareholders after the business struggled last year, reported a 23.5% increase in revenues to £69.8m in the half year to 02 July.

Everyman , which has halted new site openings this year as the business refocuses under new chief executive Farah Golant , said that admissions rose 20.5% year-on-year to 2.6m.

The cinema-going recovery, fuelled by box office hits including the latest Super Mario movie, Ryan Gosling’s Project Hail Mary and Toy Story 5 , helped Everyman bounce back to a £1.9m pre-tax profit. The company reported a £3.4m loss in the same period last year.

The strong performance meant that the company was able to reduce net debt to £17.4m, from £24.2m a year ago.

Everyman , which is opening three new venues next year, said that it increased its share of the UK market from 5.8% to 6.4% and that its membership programme increased 13.4% to 75,788.

“We have momentum and strong focus to manage the business with discipline and prudent investment,” said Golant .

The company said that it expects its financial performance this year to be “marginally ahead” of 2025, with The Odyssey and Spider-man: Brand New Day proving to be summer blockbusters, and a strong slate to round out the year including the latest releases in the Hunger Games , Avengers and Dune franchises.

Yen rallies against the dollar

In another sign that market tensions are easing, the yen is rallying against the US dollar.

The Japanese currency has gained 1.4% so far today, to ¥156.5/$, adding to a 0.9% rally yesterday.

That taken the yen/$ exchange rate away from the 160 level that tends to make policymakers jumpy.

Last month, the yan rallied thanks to a joint intervention by Washington and Tokyo. This time, though, investors are attributing the move to increased expectations of a rate hike by the Bank of Japan.

Bank of Japan (BOJ) board member Hajime Takata can take the credit, after saying yesterday the central bank should conduct interest rate hikes nimbly to counter intensifying inflationary pressures, rather than sticking to the fixed semiannual pace anticipated by markets.

Interestingly, Japan’s top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura has said that financial authorities remain on alert over currency market developments, adding:

double quotation mark “We remain on a state of heightened alert.”

stories.title: Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending
stories.summary: Speaking at the party's conference, economy spokesman Robert Jenrick says Reform will be the "party of fiscal responsibility".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 September 2026

Reform UK has pledged to cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare, net zero policies, overseas aid and the number of civil servants.

Speaking from the party's conference in Birmingham, economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said he would like to cut taxes in Reform's first Budget if it wins power at the next election but would have to "earn the trust" of the markets first.

Reform would be the "party of fiscal responsibility", he said and promised to make "big changes... in a careful way, not a cack-handed way".

Labour said the proposed cuts were "incredibly reckless and could mean vital public services like hospitals, schools and law enforcement are put at risk".

The bulk of Reform's proposed cuts come from its previously announced plans to reduce the welfare budget by £50bn.

£10bn would be saved by cutting net zero programmes while £8bn would come from reducing the civil service and £7.1bn from capping the foreign aid budget.

The party says its immigration policies, including abolishing indefinite leave to remain, would result in further savings.

Does Reform's plan to cut £50bn in welfare spending add up? Published 17 August

Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants Published 22 September 2025

Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference Published 1 day ago

Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and £45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility .

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost £15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a £5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

stories.body:
Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.

The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.

China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air .

The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February .

How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.

The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.

This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.

In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.

after newsletter promotion

Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta , the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”

Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.

In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.

Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember , which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.

“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

stories.body:
Number of new jobs being added has been fluctuating, with private companies adding 38,000 jobs in August

The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market.

The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November, according to new data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Despite the relative stability of the unemployment rate, the number of new jobs added to the economy has been fluctuating, going from 214,000 in March down to a 21,000 gain in July and then back up in August.

Figures for job growth in June and July were both revised up. After revisions, job growth in June was 31,000 jobs, up from an initial 20,000, and July was revised up by 44,000 jobs, from an initially reported loss of 23,000 to a gain of 21,000.

Economists had predicted gains would be at least 50,000 new jobs. Earlier in the week, the payroll firm ADP reported private companies added 38,000 jobs in August, lower than initial expectations and the lowest month for new jobs since January. Meanwhile, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that layoffs have been going down and are 41% lower than cuts that were announced by this time last year.

Economists have pointed out that the labor market appears to be stalled in a “slow hire, slow fire” state, with neither growth nor contractions in jobs.

A separate BLS report from earlier this week showed job openings and layoffs had changed little in July. The number of people quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting workers are feeling less confident about their ability to find another job.

For many Americans feeling frustrated about the economy, a lackluster job market feels especially painful when paired with rising prices. US inflation has increased significantly since the start of the war with Iran, with the annual inflation rate going from 2.4% in February to 3.4% in July . In May, price increases reached 4.2%, the highest rate since 2023.

In recent weeks, persistent inflation has started to have a domino effect in the US economy after a sell-off in the US bond market. Yields for US Treasury bonds have been going up since the start of the Iran war, suggesting that investors are concerned about the long-term health of the economy. Higher yields could push up the price of loans, including mortgages, car loans and the interest rate on student debt, making things even more costly for Americans.

Economists are expecting at least one interest rate hike from the US Federal Reserve before the end of the year. Higher interest rates could help lower inflation, but at the risk of destabilizing the labor market.

Last week, Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, gave his debut speech at the Fed’s symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where he said the Fed was still committed to getting inflation down to its 2% target rate, but held off on making any firm suggestions on the central bank’s next move.

“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”

Donald Trump on Friday celebrated the new job figures and threatened to “stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Fed doesn’t lower interest rates.

“A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE –IT’S A BETTER CREDIT… Very simple!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like ‘the old days’.”

stories.title: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election
stories.summary: The Green Party leader intends to run in the Holborn and St Pancras seat following Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as MP.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Zack Polanski has not been an MP in the UK Parliament before

Published 3 September 2026

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP.

Polanski, who is currently a London Assembly member but not a member of Parliament, said he was "so excited by the prospect" of being the first Green MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

The Greens are targeting the seat, until now a Labour stronghold, after coming second to Labour in the area in local elections earlier this year.

Sir Keir announced on Tuesday that he was quitting as MP for the London constituency, two months after he stood down as prime minister, setting up a challenging by-election for his successor Andy Burnham.

In comments to the Camden New Journal , external on Thursday morning, Polanski said: "I have lived and worked in this community over many years, I know it well and I love it."

"It's a clear fight between Labour and the Green Party," he added.

Polanski has already been out campaigning in the constituency despite there being no decision on who the Green candidate will be until next week.

In an interview with the BBC, he said: "We had a huge surge here in [local elections] in May. This is somewhere we can win."

He said he wanted to be the Greens' sixth MP so he could "challenge Burnham constructively".

In order to officially be the Green candidate for the seat, Polanski needs to be selected by local party members - something his comments suggest will happen.

But there have been reports in recent days of splits among local Green activists, some of whom are said to favour a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent.

Andrew Feinstein, the independent runner-up to Sir Keir in the constituency at the 2024 general election, has appeared to back Polanski's candidacy as he ruled out running himself.

Writing on X, Feinstein said: "Unfortunately I am not in a position to stand this time round."

He said the Camden People's Alliance will meet next week to formally decide its position, adding: "This is a crucial time for progressives in Camden and across the country to be united."

A date has not yet been set for the by-election.

The stakes were already high for Labour at this by-election, because it offers an early test of Burnham's ability to stave off the Green threat in inner-city constituencies.

With Polanski's candidacy, the stakes are even higher for the Greens, to see whether they make good on their leader's oft-stated ambition to replace Labour.

Polanski said a Green victory would be a "clear message that we won't sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top".

The London Assembly, on which Polanski currently sits, is an elected body of 25 representatives who scrutinise the policies of the mayor of London .

Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP Published 3 days ago

Sir Keir had been MP for the area since 2015, but said he was quitting to focus on a role in international affairs.

The former prime minister had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But he said it was the "right time" for him to "pass the baton to a successor".

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

Labour has not decided its candidate to potentially take on Polanski, with applications closing on Friday.

stories.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
stories.summary: Andy Burnham has committed to reaching the Nato target of 3.5% spending by 2035, but not 3% by 2030.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch giving a speech on defence

Published 3 September 2026

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "kicking defence spending into the long grass" as she set out Tory plans to push the figure to 3% of GDP by 2030.

Badenoch said a Conservative government would fund the commitment, worth £10bn a year, through measures including reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars.

Pointing to the threat from countries like Russia and Iran, Badenoch told a press conference: "Conflict is coming, we must act now."

So far Andy Burnham's government has only committed to setting out a plan in the spring to meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

Speaking at an event in central London, Badenoch said: "Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass.

"Our enemies are not going to sit around and wait for Labour to find the money to fight them."

Burnham has pointed to his choice of Chancellor, John Healey, who quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, as proof of his commitment to defence investment.

However, Badenoch said the prime minister should call a general election if he is not willing to find the money now, adding that Healey's decision to quit over defence spending appeared to have changed since he became chancellor.

"He resigned because Britain was not on track to reach 3% by 2030 and I praised him at the time for that decision," she said.

"Now that he is chancellor he does not seem to believe that any more and I am concerned he has been bought off with a promotion."

Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge Published 1 day ago

Badenoch accuses Starmer of leaving defence spending 'mess' for Burnham Published 1 July

Starmer dithering over defence spending, says Badenoch Published 10 June

Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April , meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving £1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with £37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.
